items.title: Inverted-U is more nuanced than the textbook curve
items.claim: The Yerkes-Dodson law (1908) proposes an inverted-U relationship between arousal and performance. What is the modern refinement?

options.text: Optimal arousal varies with task complexity (simple tasks tolerate higher arousal) and skill level. Hanin's Individual Zones of Optimal Functioning (IZOF, 1980s) shows the optimal level varies between individuals
Arousal has no effect on performance

items.reveal_title: Inverted-U, but where the peak sits varies
items.reveal:
Yerkes and Dodson's original 1908 study used mice learning brightness discrimination. The 'law' has been extended far beyond its evidence base.

Yuri Hanin's IZOF model treats optimal arousal as individual: some elite athletes perform best when relaxed, others when highly aroused. The catastrophe theory (Hardy & Fazey, 1987) adds that under high cognitive anxiety, performance can collapse sharply rather than smoothly.
items.why: A single curve hides large individual differences. Coaches who treat arousal management as one-size-fits-all miss what makes elite athletes different.

items.title: HM could form new procedural but not episodic memories
items.claim: Henry Molaison (HM) had bilateral medial temporal lobe resection in 1953 for severe epilepsy. After the operation:

options.text: He had no memory of any kind
He could not form new conscious (declarative) memories but could acquire procedural skills like mirror-tracing — improving with practice while denying ever having done the task
He recovered fully within a year
He became a famous psychologist himself

items.reveal:
Brenda Milner began studying HM in 1955. Her 1962 paper documented procedural learning despite dense anterograde amnesia. HM died in 2008; his identity was revealed posthumously. His brain was sliced into 2,401 sections (Annese et al. 2014) and photographed, available online.

His case established that medial temporal lobe (especially hippocampus) is essential for new declarative memory formation but not for procedural learning. Suzanne Corkin worked with HM for 46 years.
items.why: Single-case neuropsychology can produce findings that constrain theories of normal cognition for generations. The dissociation between memory systems was visible in one patient.

items.title: P-hacking inflates apparent significance
items.claim: Simmons, Nelson and Simonsohn's 2011 'False-Positive Psychology' demonstrated that researchers can produce a 'significant' result for almost any hypothesis. How?

options.text: Through flexibility in data analysis: collecting more data after seeing p > 0.05, dropping outliers post-hoc, choosing between dependent variables, running multiple subgroups — even without intent to deceive
By using the wrong statistical software
By having too large a sample

items.reveal:
Simmons et al. showed that using a few common research practices (optional stopping, choice between similar DVs, controlling for covariates), false positive rates could rise from 5% to over 60%.

Gelman and Loken (2014) called this the 'garden of forking paths' — even without explicit p-hacking, the path through analysis can be contingent on data in ways that inflate apparent significance. Preregistration commits researchers to choices before seeing data.
items.why: P-hacking can produce false positives without anyone meaning to do anything wrong. The fix is structural: preregister, separate exploratory from confirmatory analysis, use larger samples.
